steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on DyRA, a small network that picks an image-specific resolution scale factor for existing object detectors. Motivate the scale-variation problem, survey the ways resolution has been optimized, then introduce our network, its two losses, why it is portable, and the headline results.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Scale variation hurts detection accuracy
  - deep learning strong in CV: detection, segmentation (cite each)
  - consistent real-world accuracy hard: instance size variability (cite)
  - size variation significant in detection -> accuracy robustness vulnerable (cite)
  - fixes: optimize architecture (cite) or augment input data (cite)
  - resolution adjustment in augmentation: works without changing architecture
- Why changing resolution helps (Fig. 1)
  - detectors scale-variant: extreme large/small objects not well identified
  - resize images with huge/tiny objects to lower/higher resolution = match detector's original capacity
  - proper adjustment -> better accuracy; main focus of this work
  - careful resolution choice -> richer features; resolution is crucial hyper-parameter (cite)
- Three existing ways to optimize resolution
  - (1) predefined resolutions as augmentation (cite); also for transformer-based nets (cite)
    - dynamic resolution network (cite) picks one of these sizes
    - drawback: manual candidate resolutions, expert knowledge, trial and error
  - (2) automated augmentation search (cite): optimized resolution per image or box
  - (3) run-time adaptive scaling (cite): on the fly, no domain-specific knowledge
- DyRA: a portable image scaler (Fig. 2(a))
  - portable run-time adaptive scaling network, image-specific scale factor
  - plugs into existing detector; input = image, output = single scale factor
  - separate companion network, convolution + transformer blocks
  - jointly trained with conventional detector -> scale factor maximizes detector performance, input-specific
- Two new losses (Fig. 2(b))
  - images contain several different-sized objects -> hard to pick one factor good for all
  - ParetoScaleLoss: minimize accuracy drop from size variation; Pareto optimality (cite) + MLE (cite) from ScaleLoss (box-specific factor)
  - box-level factor enlarged/reduced by box size
  - BalanceLoss: shifts overall factor by localization performance -> network-aware
  - result: scale robustness + detector performance
- Portability and continuous scale factor
  - after training: portable to existing detectors, no domain-specific knowledge of inputs
  - Hao et al. (cite): scaling decision not transferable, whole network adapted by resized image
  - first to dynamically optimize the hyper-parameter in a fully separable network, end-to-end
  - continuous scale factor, extensive coverage -> higher performance
  - few discrete sizes -> distribution mismatch (resolution is continuous)
- Results
  - datasets: MS-COCO, PascalVOC, DOTA (cite each)
  - COCO AP gains vs multi-resolution strategy: RetinaNet 1.4%, Faster R-CNN 1.0%, FCOS 1.5%, DINO 1.5%, H-deforamble-DETR 1.2% (cite each)
  - PascalVOC / DOTA: Faster-RCNN AP +1.8% / +2.3%

steps.text:
Deep learning has shown very good performance in computer vision tasks like object detection and segmentation. But it is still a challenge to get consistent accuracy in real-world applications, because the sizes of instances vary a lot. In object detection the size variation is often significant, and this can make the robustness of the accuracy vulnerable. Several solutions have been proposed for this problem, either optimizing the neural network architecture or augmenting the input data. Among data augmentation methods, adjusting the resolution can address the problem effectively and it does not need any change to the network architecture.

Fig. 1 shows why changing the image resolution can improve the detection accuracy. Detection networks have scale-variant performance, so objects with extreme sizes, either large or small, are not identified well. To alleviate this, the image that contains huge or tiny objects can be resized to a lower or higher resolution, which means matching the resolution to the original capacity of the detector, and this can help the network to recognize the objects more efficiently. If the resolution of the image is adjusted properly, the detection accuracy will be enhanced effectively, and this is the main focus of this work. Also, choosing the resolution carefully can let the network extract richer information, since the resolution is a crucial hyper-parameter for network performance.

There are several approaches for optimizing the resolution, and they can be classified into three. The first one scales the input images with predefined resolutions and applies them as data augmentation to the networks, and this can also be applied to transformer-based networks. The dynamic resolution network allows adaptive resolution by selecting one of these sizes. However, the obvious drawback of this approach is that the candidate resolutions have to be determined by manual work, which relies on expert knowledge and needs lots of trial and error. To remove the need for human expertise, the second approach, automated augmentation search, was proposed, and it enables an optimized resolution for each image or box. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has shown very good performance in computer vision tasks like object detection and segmentation. But it is still a challenge to get consistent accuracy in real-world applications, because the sizes of instances vary a lot. In object detection the size variation is often significant, and this can make the robustness of the accuracy vulnerable. Several solutions have been proposed for this problem, either optimizing the neural network architecture or augmenting the input data. Among data augmentation methods, adjusting the resolution can address the problem effectively and it does not need any change to the network architecture.

Fig. 1 shows why changing the image resolution can improve the detection accuracy. Detection networks have scale-variant performance, so objects with extreme sizes, either large or small, are not identified well. To alleviate this, the image that contains huge or tiny objects can be resized to a lower or higher resolution, which means matching the resolution to the original capacity of the detector, and this can help the network to recognize the objects more efficiently. If the resolution of the image is adjusted properly, the detection accuracy will be enhanced effectively, and this is the main focus of this work. Also, choosing the resolution carefully can let the network extract richer information, since the resolution is a crucial hyper-parameter for network performance.

There are several approaches for optimizing the resolution, and they can be classified into three. The first one scales the input images with predefined resolutions and applies them as data augmentation to the networks, and this can also be applied to transformer-based networks. The dynamic resolution network allows adaptive resolution by selecting one of these sizes. However, the obvious drawback of this approach is that the candidate resolutions have to be determined by manual work, which relies on expert knowledge and needs lots of trial and error. To remove the need for human expertise, the second approach, automated augmentation search, was proposed, and it enables an optimized resolution for each image or box. The last approach is run-time adaptive scaling, which optimizes the resolution on the fly without domain-specific knowledge.

In this paper we propose DyRA, a portable run-time adaptive scaling network that produces a scale factor specific to the image. Fig. 2(a) shows how the image scaler can be plugged into an existing detector. The input of the scaler module is the image and its output is a single scale factor for the resolution. DyRA is a separate companion neural network made of convolution and transformer blocks, and it is trained jointly with a conventional object detector. Because the two networks are trained jointly, the scale factor can be optimized to maximize the detector performance while the network learns the input-specific scale factor.

Two new loss functions are used when training DyRA, and they are shown in Fig. 2(b). An image usually has several objects of different sizes, so it is hard to decide one scale factor that gives an accuracy gain for all of the instances. So ParetoScaleLoss tries to minimize the accuracy drop caused by the size variation, using Pareto optimality and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) from ScaleLoss, which is for a box-specific scale factor. The box-level scale factor is optimized by enlarging or reducing it depending on the given box size. BalanceLoss changes the position of the overall scale factor based on the localization performance, so that the scale factor is network-aware. With these loss functions the scale factor can be optimized for scale robustness while the performance of the detector is also considered.

Unlike prior approaches, once DyRA is trained it is highly portable to existing detectors and does not need domain-specific knowledge about the input data. For example, the automatic scaling decision of Hao et al. cannot be transferred to other detectors, because the whole neural network is adapted by the resized image. As far as we know, DyRA is the first attempt to dynamically optimize the hyper-parameter in a network that is fully separable from existing networks, in an end-to-end manner. In addition, our network gives a continuous scale factor with extensive scale coverage, which results in higher detection performance. This is important because the resolution has a continuous range, and selecting from only a few discrete sizes can cause a distribution mismatch.

We verified the proposed approach with various object detectors on MS-COCO, PascalVOC, and DOTA. On COCO, compared to the multi-resolution strategy, the AP (average precision) improved by 1.4% on RetinaNet, 1.0% on Faster R-CNN, 1.5% on FCOS, 1.5% on DINO, and 1.2% on H-deforamble-DETR. On PascalVOC and DOTA, the AP of Faster-RCNN was enhanced by 1.8% and 2.3%.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep learning has demonstrated remarkable performance in computer vision applications such as object detection [1,2] and segmentation [3,4]. However, achieving consistent accuracy in real-world applications is still a challenge because of the variability of instance sizes [5,6,7]. In object detection the variation in size is often significant, which can make the robustness of accuracy vulnerable [8]. Several solutions have been proposed to address this problem, either by optimizing the architecture of neural networks [9,10,7] or by augmenting the input data [11,12,8]. In data augmentation, resolution adjustment can effectively address the problem without changing the network architecture.

Fig. 1 illustrates why varying image resolution can improve detection accuracy. Because detection networks have scale-variant performance, objects with extreme sizes, either large or small, are not well identified. To alleviate this shortcoming, resizing an image containing huge or tiny objects to a lower or higher resolution, i.e., matching the resolution to the original capacity of the detector, can help the network recognize objects more efficiently. If the resolution of the image is properly adjusted, the detection accuracy will be effectively enhanced, and this is the main focus of this work. Moreover, careful resolution selection can lead the network to extract richer information, since the resolution is a crucial hyper-parameter for the performance of networks [13,14].

There are several approaches to optimizing the resolution, which can be classified into three. The first is to scale the input images with predefined resolutions and apply them as data augmentation to the networks [11,8], which is also applicable to transformer-based networks [15,16,17,18]. The dynamic resolution network [19] allows adaptive resolution by selecting one of these sizes. However, an obvious drawback of this approach is that candidate resolutions must be determined manually, relying on expert knowledge with lots of trial and error. To eliminate this need for human expertise, the second approach, automated augmentation search [6], has been proposed to enable an optimized resolution for each image or box. The last is run-time adaptive scaling [20], which optimizes the resolution on the fly without domain-specific knowledge.

In this paper, we propose DyRA, a portable run-time adaptive scaling network that produces an image-specific scale factor. Fig. 2(a) illustrates how the proposed image scaler can be plugged into an existing detector. Note that the input to the scaler module is the image, and its output is a single scale factor for the resolution. DyRA is designed as a separate companion neural network with convolution and transformer blocks and is trained jointly with a conventional object detector. By jointly training the two networks, the scale factor can be optimized to maximize the performance of the detector while learning the input-specific scale factor.

Two newly designed loss functions, depicted in Fig. 2(b), are applied when training DyRA. An image typically includes several objects of different sizes, which makes it hard to decide on a scale factor that provides an accuracy gain for all instances. Hence, ParetoScaleLoss aims to minimize the accuracy drop caused by size variation by employing Pareto optimality [21] and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) [22] from ScaleLoss, which is for the box-specific scale factor. The box-level scale factor is optimized by enlarging or reducing it based on the given box size. BalanceLoss adjusts the position of the overall scale factor based on localization performance so that the scale factor is network-aware. Through these loss functions, the scale factor can be optimized for scale robustness while taking the performance of the detector into account.

Different from prior approaches, once trained, DyRA is highly portable to existing detectors without domain-specific knowledge about the input data. For instance, the automatic scaling decision in Hao et al. [20] is not transferable to other detectors, because the entire neural network is adapted by the resized image. To the best of our knowledge, DyRA is the first attempt to dynamically optimize the hyper-parameter in a network fully separable from existing networks in an end-to-end manner. Furthermore, our network yields a continuous scale factor offering extensive scale coverage, which results in higher detection performance. This matters because the resolution has a continuous range, and selecting from a few discrete sizes can lead to a distribution mismatch.

We verified the effectiveness of the proposed approach with various object detectors on MS-COCO [23], PascalVOC [24], and DOTA [25]. On COCO, compared to the multi-resolution strategy, detectors achieved an AP (average precision) improvement of 1.4% on RetinaNet [26], 1.0% on Faster R-CNN [27], 1.5% on FCOS [28], 1.5% on DINO [29], and 1.2% on H-deforamble-DETR [30].
